name: Kodunkundreesar Temple, Piranmalai (Thirukodunkundram)
deity: Shiva as Kodunkundreesar, with the goddess Kuyilamudhanayagi; on the summit as Mangai Bagar, in wedding form
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Pandya Nadu on a sacred hill, sung by Sambandar in the Tevaram (7th century)
dynasty: Pandya country; a hill long associated with the Sangam chieftain Pari
style: Dravidian, with shrines on three levels of the hill
summary: On the steep hill of Piranmalai, the Thirukodunkundram of the Tevaram, Shiva is worshipped on three levels — Kodunkundreesar at the foot, Bhairava midway, and on the summit the Lord and Parvati in their wedding form.

sections.history: Piranmalai is a hill village in Sivaganga district, and its temple is the Thirukodunkundram — the shrine of the steep hill — that Thirugnana Sambandar sang. It is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and is counted fifth among the fourteen of Pandya Nadu. The hill carries memories older than the Tevaram: tradition identifies it with Parambu, the hill country of Pari, the Sangam-age chieftain remembered among the seven great patrons of Tamil poetry for his boundless generosity, and the name Piranmalai is said to have grown out of Parambu Malai. Arunagirinathar later sang of Murugan here too.
sections.architecture: The temple climbs the hill in three tiers, which tradition likens to the lower world, the earth and Kailasa. At the foot stands the main temple of Kodunkundreesar and the goddess Kuyilamudhanayagi. Midway is a shrine of Viswanathar and Visalakshi, closely associated with Bhairava, who has his own fierce shrine on the hill. On the summit, reached by a long climb, Shiva and Parvati are enshrined together as Mangai Bagar. Rock-cut pools known as the Pandava theerthams are carved into the hill.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that Vayu, the wind, and Adisesha, the cosmic serpent, once tested their strength at Mount Meru, and the fragments the wind tore away fell to earth as sacred hills — this among them. When Shiva wed Parvati, Agastya was sent south to balance the earth, and was promised the sight of the wedding wherever he wished; on this summit he is said to have received it. The summit image is held to be made of herbal substances, so it receives no abhishekam, only fragrant civet oil on Fridays.
sections.festivals: Bhairava's shrine draws special worship in the Tamil month of Thai, and the Shaiva festivals of the year — Pradosham, Maha Shivaratri and the days of the goddess — are kept at the foot of the hill. For many devotees the climb to the summit is itself the pilgrimage. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Begin at the foot with Kodunkundreesar and the goddess, then climb: the steps rise past the Bhairava shrine to the summit, where the wedding form of Shiva and Parvati rewards the effort with wide views over the plains. The climb is long and steep in places, so start early, carry water, and allow most of a morning.

visit.timings: The temple at the foot of the hill is open in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure; ask there about access to the shrines on the hill. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside the shrines. Sturdy footwear for the path up the hill is advisable.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctums; on the hill and in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Piranmalai lies in Sivaganga district, a short drive from Singampunari and about 65 km by road north-east of Madurai; buses run from Singampunari and Thiruppathur. Madurai is the nearest airport and major railhead, with Karaikudi also within reach.
